resources. In short, it means that we must recognize our old
way of life to be sinful.
In the passage in which Luther says that belief in God as
Creator is the central, decisive, all-embracing belief, and
in which he adds that there are few "who have progressed
so far as to believe in the fullest sense that our God is the
God who creates and makes all things", he continues thus:
"For such a man must be dead to all things, to good and ill,
to life and death, to heaven and hell, and must from the
depths of his heart confess that in his own strength he can do
nothing."
The man who is able to confess this is also able to realize
what a gift God has given to the world in Jesus Christ. Such
a one encounters Jesus as the manifestation of the redeeming
grace of God in this world, and the word which promises
this grace to the sinner finds its way into his heart. All this
is made vividly clear to us in our story. When Peter in
obedience to the command of Jesus has let down his net and
made the wonderful catch of fish, he falls to his knees before
Jesus and says: "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man,
O Lord." Jesus, however, does not reject his adoration
but promises: "Do not be afraid; henceforth you will be
catching men." Thus to the prostrate sinner the miracle is
made known, and the real miracle is just this—that Jesus
calls to His service sinful man, that He transforms the being
of sinful man making him a new and pure creation.
In fact the one and the true miracle is that the word of
God's saving grace which meets us in Jesus Christ creates us
anew, freeing us from the fetters of ourselves and our old
sinful way of life, thereby making us a "new creation". The
fact that this word of grace goes on resounding, that it
challenges us even to-day, here and now, with the question
whether we are prepared to understand our whole life in the
light of this divine word—just that is the revelation to us of
God's rule as Creator.
